Adult female Chiricahua leopard frogs attain a maximum snout–vent length of 13.7 centimeters [Li = 13.7 centimeters], a size that markedly exceeds the 11.2 centimeters [Li = 11.2 centimeters] recorded as the ultimate SVL for males of this species. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism is typical among ranid frogs and likely reflects the selective advantage of larger body size in females for clutch volume production. Hatchlings emerge from their gelatinous egg masses at a remarkably small size, with a wet weight at birth of only 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams]. The incubation period is relatively prolonged under the cooler conditions typical of montane breeding sites; embryos maintained at a constant temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] require approximately 40 days [ab = approximately 40 days] to complete development and hatch. This slow developmental rate is consistent with the species' reliance on thermally stable, spring-fed pools in the high-elevation streams of the Sky Islands region.

Upon hatching, the free-swimming tadpoles undergo a period of rapid growth and development that culminates in metamorphosis. The snout–vent length at metamorphosis averages 3.9 centimeters , which represents a substantial increase from the newly hatched larva. Metamorphosing individuals transition from an aquatic, filter-feeding Gosner-stage larva to a terrestrial juvenile froglet, a process that involves extensive body plan reorganisation including tail resorption and limb bud development. The larval stage duration, and consequently the size at metamorphic climax, can vary considerably depending on local thermal and nutritional conditions. Reaching this developmental milestone is a critical juncture in the life cycle, as the post-metamorphic juvenile must immediately begin foraging on small terrestrial invertebrates to build the energy reserves necessary for survival through the first winter. This transition from the aquatic tadpole to the terrestrial juvenile marks a fundamental shift in both habitat use and feeding ecology.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs at a comparatively small body size relative to the ultimate adult dimensions. Both sexes achieve puberty at a snout–vent length of 4.6 centimeters [Lp = 4.6 centimeters], a value common to both females and males. Reaching this length initiates gametogenesis and the development of secondary sexual characteristics, notably the enlargement of the tympanum in males and the onset of vitellogenesis in females. Despite attaining reproductive maturity at this modest size, individuals continue to grow throughout their lives, and the largest adults are typically several years old. The delay in achieving full adult body size relative to the onset of sexual maturity is a common life-history pattern among temperate anurans and may reflect the high energetic demands of reproduction, which compete with somatic growth in reproductively active adults. Once puberty is reached, breeding activity is contingent upon suitable environmental conditions, particularly adequate rainfall and appropriate water temperatures.

Under favourable thermal conditions at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], this species exhibits a remarkably high reproductive output for a temperate ranid. Individual females can produce up to approximately 257 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 257 eggs per clutch], and they may deposit multiple clutches during a single breeding season. The maximum observed clutch frequency reaches about 54.7 clutches per year [F_R_i = about 54.7 clutches per year], a rate that likely represents the upper physiological limit under optimal conditions. This level of fecundity, when considered alongside the species' moderate body size, is consistent with a life-history strategy that emphasises high reproductive effort to offset potentially high mortality rates in the larval and juvenile stages. The eggs are deposited in shallow, vegetated pools where they are attached to submerged vegetation, and the entire clutch is enveloped in a protective gelatinous matrix. Developing embryos are vulnerable to desiccation, predation by aquatic invertebrates, and fungal infections, all of which exert strong selective pressure on egg mass placement.

The ultimate wet weight for females reaches approximately 257 grams [Wwi = approximately 257 grams], while adult males attain a substantially lower maximum body mass of around 140 grams [Wwi = around 140 grams]. This pronounced difference in mass, even greater than the divergence in SVL, underscores the substantial energetic investment that females make in egg production. The maximum recorded longevity for this species under warm conditions of 28 °C [T = 28 °C] is approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years], a lifespan that is relatively long compared to many other North American ranids of similar body size. This extended lifespan may be linked to the species' reliance on permanent, spring-fed aquatic habitats that buffer against extreme climatic fluctuations, thereby reducing the risk of catastrophic mortality. Comparative data from related species suggest that individuals in cooler, high-elevation populations may live even longer by allocating more energy to somatic maintenance and less to annual reproductive output, though direct measurements of age structure in wild populations remain limited.
